title: How to Kill the Code Review — Ankit Jain, Aviator
talk_summary: Ankit argues code review's bottleneck is not just bug-catching but alignment, and proposes capturing agent-session decisions as acceptance criteria, converting recurring review comments into an 'AI slop registry' of guardrails, and reviewing verification evidence rather than line-by-line diffs. He also recommends deterministic checks where possible with LLM fallback, and warns against letting the same agent write code and its test plan.

takeaways.what_they_do: Mine historical review comments for repeatable defects, codify them as repo-specific rules/checks, and feed them to reviewers so the same comment is not re-raised.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Every recurring comment is now a guardrail that you don't have to review again.
capture the user responses and that essentially forms your acceptance criteria

takeaways.technique: Review intent and evidence, not diff
takeaways.what_they_do: Make the review surface intent plus acceptance criteria plus verification artifacts such as screenshots, DB snapshots, and test results, not line-by-line code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: now reviewers are reviewing the intent, not the diff.

takeaways.what_they_do: Use deterministic checks for criteria where possible; use LLM/agent browsing and screenshots only for ambiguous behavior.
takeaways.evidence_quote: deterministic where it can be, but LLM where you must.

takeaways.what_they_do: Build the test plan from session/acceptance criteria, not from the same agent that wrote the code, to avoid self-review blind spots.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if your code is built by the same agent which is actually building a test plan, it's not going to build a test plan which will actually catch issues.

takeaways.technique: Plain-English acceptance criteria as shared surface
takeaways.what_they_do: Write acceptance criteria and test plans in plain English so PM/designers and agents can review intent before or alongside code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the test plan is now something which even you can share with your product managers, your designers.
